body.text: In short:
Anti-violence advocates want the Murray Plains candidate to withdraw from the election over historic conduct breaches.
Garner Smith commented on a video of Dustin Martin allegedly touching a woman's breasts in 2022.
What's next?
Victorian One Nation leader Warren Pickering says he continues to support Garner Smith.

Anti-violence campaigners are calling for a One Nation candidate to withdraw from the Victorian election campaign over historic comments on a video of a former AFL player allegedly touching a shirtless woman's breasts in a hospitality venue.
Gannawarra Shire councillor Garner Smith, who is contesting Murray Plains, wrote "I'd be more worried if he didn't go in for a feel" on the 2022 video post of Richmond player Dustin Martin.
Later on the same post, Mr Smith told those offended to "buy a bag of cement and harden the #@&! up".
When asked by the ABC whether he stood by those comments now, four years on, Mr Smith denied their relevance.
"Look, there are just bigger ticket items to deal with," Mr Smith said.
"I did not pass any opinion on women."
When asked if he was denying making the comments, Mr Smith said: "No, I'm just saying that there's no comment about women at all on it."
Mr Smith declined a further interview to discuss his comments, stating there were more important issues to focus on, including agricultural jobs, water politics and electricity costs.
The AFL's integrity department assessed the video, which was filmed in 2015 but only made public in 2022, and decided not to sanction Martin over his conduct.
Smith 'did not take any responsibility'
The deputy mayor of Gannawarra Shire Council at the time, Jane Ogden, raised concerns about Mr Smith's comments in 2022.

She moved a council motion seeking an arbiter to investigate whether the comments breached the councillor Standards of Conduct set out in Schedule 1 of the Local Government (Governance and Integrity) Regulations 2020.
In March 2023, arbiter Yehudi Blacher found Mr Smith's comments breached five standards:
• discrimination, sexual harassment and victimisation in accordance with the Equal Opportunity Act 2010;
• failure to promote gender equality;
• obscene behaviour in dealings with the members of the public;
• failure to treat all persons with respect; and
• bringing discredit upon the council.
The arbiter directed Mr Smith to publicly apologise to the Gannawarra community, issue the apology to relevant local media within seven days, and table it at the next council meeting.
Mr Smith tabled a written apology at a council meeting on April 19, 2023.
"My comment related to defending an action of Dustin Martin. An action not considered an offence in the eyes of the law, not an offence in the eyes of the AFL integrity department," he wrote.
"All evidence suggests that he has done nothing wrong in the eyes of the vast majority of the public. Yet, the media tried to profit from the issue and failed.
"To everyday people, it is clear that the woman was working in a professional capacity and Dustin Martin is only guilty of doing something hardly surprising under the circumstances.

"I apologise to the Shire of Gannawarra community for my postings on this matter. My interpretation of the arbiter's decision is that an apology would not be necessary if I had begun my comment with 'I am a councillor of the Gannawarra Shire, but this is strictly my option [sic]'."
The arbiter also directed Mr Smith to undertake training in the proper use of social media.
Gannawarra Shire Council declined to answer whether or not Mr Smith had completed that training.
The ABC asked Mr Smith directly, but he did not respond.
Ms Ogden has since described the apology as "very insincere".
"He just never acknowledged and took responsibility for making that comment, just blamed it on that there was absolutely nothing wrong with what the AFL player did," she said.
"I'm just really sad … just that someone that doesn't have many ethics around things like that has continued to be voted back in as a councillor and that he's now running for One Nation.
"He did not take any responsibility for his comments."
'It just normalises misogyny'

Australian Femicide Watch and Red Heart Movement founder Sherele Moody said Mr Smith's progression from councillor to mayor and now state election candidate, after the comments he made, was "deeply disturbing".
She rejected the concept that other issues should be prioritised over women's safety.
"Misogyny is a really important thing for all Australians to be focused on,"
Ms Moody said.
"Particularly people who are entering politics because they have a chance to actually make decisions that can ultimately change the way that men and boys view women in Australia."
Ms Moody said allowing men to retain public platforms after making comments such as Mr Smith's normalises demeaning attitudes towards women.
"When men make these comments and they're allowed to keep the pedestal they're standing on, it just normalises misogyny and reduces women to sex objects."
She called on Mr Smith to apologise for the remarks.
"The best response from him would have been, 'I'm sorry that I said that, that was wrong and I will never do it again'."
Wimmera woman and chief executive of anti-violence organisation It's Never Okay Kim O'Reilly said Mr Smith should not hold a position of power in which he represented communities.
"He should not be allowed to speak for others," Ms O'Reilly said.
The ABC has seen correspondence between Ms O'Reilly and the Gannawarra Shire Council in 2022 about Mr Smith's comments.
A council employee responded to Ms O'Reilly, saying: "Most of our councillors are appalled by Cr Smith's comments and behaviour."
However, councillors elected him as mayor two years later in 2024 and re-elected him in 2025.
"There's never going to be a consequence or there's never going to be a change unless the enabling stops,"
Ms O'Reilly said.
'Chauvinistic' and 'sexist'

Mr Smith and One Nation Victoria leader Warren Pickering did not respond to the ABC's request for a response to criticisms from anti-violence advocates, including the calls for an apology and for One Nation to reconsider Mr Smith's candidacy.
Addressing a room of journalists at a Melbourne Press Club and Rural Press Club event, Mr Pickering said he was confident Mr Smith was "genuinely sorry" for his "sexist" and "chauvinistic" comments.
He commended Mr Smith for being transparent about his comments.
"I think if you are open and honest about them when you do come forward, look, I think that's a green flag, not a red one," Mr Pickering said.
Scrutiny of Mr Smith's comments came as other Victorian One Nation candidates were being criticised for their remarks about women and girls.
The party's Shepparton candidate Phil Bryant described coaching girls' netball teams and working with women as "herding chickens" at his campaign launch last week.
Mr Pickering and Mr Bryant did not respond to the ABC's media inquiries.
At the start of November, One Nation's Melbourne candidate Matthew Collins resigned and apologised after offensive comments posted on his social media accounts came to light.
The comments reportedly ranged from highly sexualised remarks to anti-Muslim rhetoric.
Mr Collins released a statement via the party apologising for his past statements.
